review_text: Who thought that starting off boring and empty before a suddenly exponential difficulty curve was a good idea? The music is well-made, though the leitmotif is perhaps too forward in most tracks, and the pixel art is gorgeous, but in terms of actual gameplay there's just too much of a focus on huge spaces and tiny things occupying them, from your character to all of the incoming threats, and the soon-cluttered UI is no great help. Even better is the way that settings in the options menu are not saved between sessions. This game seems entirely overrated. It's not terrible, but there are far better options out there.
notes: - Thumbs down: a boring, empty start, then a sudden exponential difficulty curve.
- Well-made music, though the main theme is too forward.
- Huge spaces with tiny characters and threats in them.
- Option settings are not saved between sessions.

review_text:
First off, this is not a roguelike, nor can it be said to have "roguelike elements" either. So stop calling it one.

It is a pure action game with randomly distributed items and premade levels that have semi-randomized structures. It is close to arcade design philosophy, but not quite. Luck plays too much of a factor in item generation, which can and will make or break runs (unless you play Huntress, because, regardless of what anyone may think or say on the matter, the ability to move while attacking puts her above everyone else in the cast) Yes, it is very possible to extend past the upper limit of the difficulty timer and become an absurd missile-spewing, marathon-running, never-dying asshat. But at that point you're more or less ruining whatever is left of the experience for yourself.

What puts me off most of all is the idea of unlockables, or first and foremost, the idea that you cannot experience the game at its best until you fulfill all sorts of weird "achievements". It puts me off partly because I know some of you are going to BAWW at me for downloading a complete save, when the fact is I just cannot be bothered to deal with this ♥♥♥♥. It's a lame excuse to wring more playtime out of the player, and the less we see of it the better. I'd rather everything be unlocked from the start and the upper difficulty limit to mean certain death, even for stupidly powerful characters, but what can I do? People are just too satisfied.

I only grudgingly recommend. Play it with others.
notes: - Says it is not a roguelike and should stop being called one - a pure action game with random items and premade levels.
- Luck in the items makes or breaks runs.
- Huntress, who can move while attacking, is above the rest of the cast.
- Past the top of the difficulty timer you become an unstoppable powerhouse, which ruins what is left of the challenge.
- The game is at its best only after weird achievement unlocks - a lame way to wring out playtime.
- Downloaded a complete save file to skip the unlocks.
- Only grudgingly recommends it; play it with others.

review_text:
Bought this game because of its local co-op support and was left a bit underwhelmed. We start with two characters which didn't offer enough immediate variance between runs for three people. It felt like progression was quite slow since we only unlocked the enforcer and bandit after a couple of hours of playing.

There were some scale issues when playing on a TV since we needed enough room that we could occasionally spread out without the camera getting wonky which meant that everything was very small. In this game if you jump off a bridge, all of your friends follow you instead of the other way around.  The screen limitations completely negated at least one active item (Marble Gate), though to be honest that was kind of hilarious. It was easy to get punished by bad seeds since in local co-op the entire team needs to move as one and you can't split up to discover the gate so its possible a lot of time is wasted if you start searching the wrong direction. 

If you've already played this game single player or with online co-op and you have unlocked characters/artifacts then you're probably in for a good time. But don't expect to really unlock anything over the course of natural play when playing strictly local co-op.
notes: - Thumbs down: bought for local co-op, but two starting characters are too few for three players, and unlocks come slowly.
- On a shared TV screen the camera keeps everyone together, so everything is tiny and when one player drops off a ledge the others are dragged along.
- The whole team must move as one, so a bad start searching the wrong way for the gate wastes much time.

review_text:
Yoinked ROR1 when it came out, played it constantly back when I still had a Windows XP PC.

Properly bought ROR2 a couple of years back, turned into a completionist with 100 something hours and still trying to 100% the game alongside Eclipses.

Bit the bullet and bought RORR a few weeks back, trying to find the old feeling of ROR1 while insisting that it would be a "chilled ROR2" since I would use a controller. Nope, it's just as chaotic, and hurts my wrist immensely because of how bad I held the controller but it's too good. I felt the feeling of the original ROR again.

Love it. Still my first ever Rougelike series, the first series that managed to convince that I'm not just an FPS player, and one that I still play to this day. It better receives more update, Gearbox. <3
notes: - Felt the first game's feeling again - just as chaotic.

review_text: I have yet to get past the second level, but difficulty aside this game is well worth it. Though it may not appear to be much at first glance, there are many different characters to play as (though unlocking them may prove as difficult as the game itself!), procedurally generated levels and TONS of powerups. The learning curve is fairly low, the keyboard controls are simple and can be customized, the graphics are simple yet aesthetically pleasing and the replay value is high. Definitely worth paying full price for, but if you see it on sale and enjoy side-scrolling shoot-em-ups then do not pass it up!
notes: - Many characters, though unlocking them can be as hard as the game.
- Simple keyboard controls you can customise.

review_text:
I'm one of those scrubs who played [i]Risk of Rain 2[/i] before playing the original, aka the 99%.

Except I still haven't played the 'original' [i]RoR,[/i] instead opting for [i]Risk of Rain Returns,[/i] which has been described (perhaps accurately; I wouldn't know) as an all-around upgrade over the original [i]RoR.[/i]

Well, upgrade or not, I can confidently state this game is great.

It's like [i]RoR 2[/i] with better graphics, worse gameplay, but significantly more dopamine-inducing moments. Arguably the best 2D shooter I've ever played.

Some of the items would be absolutely bonkers to see in its sequel. Others, I'm glad were introduced into the first title after they had proven themselves in [i]Risk of Rain 2[/i]. It's really the best of both worlds.

Will I ever play the original? Honestly... Probably not, because I have a feeling this is the ideal way to experience the risk associated with rain.

9 / 10 — would get rained on again (except by the Magma worm; ♥♥♥♥ you, Magma Worm)
notes: - Like Risk of Rain 2 with better graphics and worse gameplay, but more rush-inducing moments - perhaps the best 2D shooter they have played.
- Items from both games together - the best of both worlds.
